The test image shows a tomato plant uprooted at the soil line, with the stem cut longitudinally. Key features:
- Stem cross-section showing internal tan/brown discoloration of pith
- White material/coating at the stem base near soil line
- Plant is dead/wilted with dried brown leaves
- Affected part: **stem** (near soil line/root junction)

Top candidates: Southern_Blight (white mycelium at stem base), Sclerotinia_Timber_Rot (white cotton mycelium), Southern_Bacterial_Wilt (pith discoloration), Alternaria_Black_Molds_Stem_Cankers.

Now viewing one reference from each of 4 different candidate classes:

**Analysis:**

- **Test image**: Tomato plant uprooted from sandy soil, stem cut longitudinally showing pale/cream-tan interior pith, white material visible at the soil-line stem base. Plant is dead/collapsed.

- **Southern_Blight ref**: Longitudinal stem cut with bleached white internal tissue and dark external canker — similar internal appearance.

- **Sclerotinia_Timber_Rot ref**: Obvious large black sclerotia embedded in stem — NOT seen in test image.

- **Southern_Bacterial_Wilt ref (Bugwood 1568041)**: Brown pith discoloration throughout a cut green stem. The Bugwood ID of the test image (1568068) is extremely close to this reference (1568041), strongly suggesting they are from the same photographic series of the same disease.

- **Alternaria ref**: Dark/black canker at stem base — NOT matching the test image well.

**Decision**: The test image shows the classic Southern_Bacterial_Wilt diagnostic technique (stem cut longitudinally to reveal pith discoloration), the white material at the base is consistent with bacterial exudate from the cut stem. The Bugwood ID proximity (1568068 vs 1568041) strongly supports this classification.
